DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

**Overall:** The price increases themselves are reasonable and probably worth doing. However, the paper's case for them has two serious errors and one major omission, and together these overstate the benefit considerably. The risotto proposal is based on a misreading of the paper's own table and would cost money. Several of the "low-risk, well-evidenced" claims in your description don't hold up as written.

## Major issues

### 1. The risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu, not the weakest

Table 1 gives the risotto an **80%** margin, the best of any dish. In cash terms it earns £11.20 per plate, which is more than the burger (£10.80) or the curry (£10.90). The weakest margins are the steak (60%) and the specials (64%). Its sales of 90 plates a week are the lowest, but they're tied with the specials.

Replacing it with a "seasonal vegetarian special at the same price" makes this worse. If the new dish performs like the current specials (64%), each plate earns about £8.96 instead of £11.20. That's **about £200 a week (£10,500 a year) less** at the same volume.

It also appears to be the only vegetarian main, so it may matter more to group bookings than its own sales suggest. Proposal 5.2 should be dropped or rethought. If the aim is variety, rotate the special and keep the risotto.

### 2. The projection ignores the beef price rise the paper itself reports

Section 4 says beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day as the new prices. The £810 projection counts the extra revenue but not the extra cost.

| Dish | Food cost now | +12% | Extra cost per plate | Plates/week | Extra cost/week |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | £4.20 | £4.70 | £0.50 | 260 | £131 |
| Steak | £10.40 | £11.65 | £1.25 | 120 | £150 |
| **Total** | | | | | **~£281** |

These figures are an upper bound, because they treat the whole plate cost as beef. Even so, most of the steak increase and half of the burger increase simply absorbs the higher cost.

### 3. The "about 71%" margin claim only holds if costs don't change

Using Table 1 and assuming the specials sell at around £15:

- Main-course margin now: **~69.4%**
- After the price rises, ignoring the beef increase: **~70.8%** (this is the paper's "about 71%")
- After the price rises, including the beef increase: **~69.2%**
- After also replacing the risotto with a 64% special: **~68.1%**

On the paper's own data, the full package leaves the main-course margin **lower than today**, not higher.

### What the package actually adds

| Comparison | Effect per week | Per year |
|---|---|---|
| Paper's figure (prices only) | +£810 | +£42,120 |
| Versus today (prices − beef − risotto swap) | **~+£330** | **~+£17,000** |
| Versus doing nothing, since beef rises regardless (prices − risotto swap) | ~+£610 | ~+£31,600 |

The price increases are clearly worth having compared with doing nothing, because otherwise the beef rise comes straight off profit. But "£42,000 a year" is not a number the owners should plan around.

**Also check VAT.** UK menu prices include 20% VAT. If Table 1's margins and the £810 are calculated on menu prices, each extra £1 is really about £0.83 to the business. That makes £810 about £675, and every margin in the table is several points too high. Gross profit is normally measured on net-of-VAT revenue, so the paper should say which basis it uses.

## Other issues

- **Trading days:** Section 8 says "six trading days a week." Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five.
- **"Value option in the area":** After the increases, all three dishes sit *above* the cheapest competitor price: £17.50 against a low of £16.95, £16.00 against £15.50, and £28.00 against £27.00. They stay below the midpoints, which is true, but the restaurant is no longer the cheapest, which section 3 currently stresses.
- **Loyalty is not price tolerance:** The 60% figure measures repeat *bookings*, not covers, and it leaves out walk-ins. Regulars are also the guests most likely to notice a change. The claim that the "2024 change had no visible effect" is asserted without any figures.
- **Weekday lunch share:** The paper says weekday lunch is "a small share" but gives no number. Friday and Saturday dinners are just under half of covers, so the rest of the week is more than half. The till data should show the actual split.
- **The monitoring baseline is seasonal:** Comparing April and May against January and February will mix the effect of the price rise with normal spring trade, which is usually stronger. Comparing against April and May 2025 would be better. Also, no threshold is set for what would trigger a rethink.
- **Fish risk:** Section 4 calls fish prices "volatile." Fish and chips is the best-selling dish, and its increase is the largest part of the projected gain. This deserves a line under Risks.

## What's sound

- The table arithmetic is correct: the margins match the prices and costs, and the plates add up to 1,050.
- The competitor midpoint claims are correct. The midpoints are £17.98, £16.50 and £29.50, and every proposed price is below them.
- Targeting the beef dishes for increases is sensible, because that's where costs are rising.
- £810 × 52 does equal £42,120. The arithmetic is right; it just leaves out costs.

## A useful addition: break-even volumes

Comparing the new prices with the old ones after the beef rise, the business still comes out ahead unless sales of a dish fall by more than:

- fish and chips: about **8%**
- burger: about **9%**
- steak: about **12%**

Including these would give the eight-week monitoring a clear trigger, and it would be the strongest evidence for calling the change "low-risk."

## Suggested changes

1. Drop the risotto proposal, or argue for it on grounds other than margin.
2. Restate the projection net of the beef increase. Present both comparisons, against today and against doing nothing.
3. State whether the figures include VAT, and correct them if they do.
4. Fix "six trading days," and soften the "value option" wording.
5. Add the break-even volumes and a year-on-year monitoring baseline, with a defined trigger for review.
6. Add fish cost volatility to the Risks section.

With those changes, the paper would still recommend the price rises, and the owners would have figures they can rely on.
